definition:
In Scripture the law is the instruction God gave Israel through Moses: the Ten Commandments and the statutes and ordinances gathered in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. It was given to a people God had already rescued. The Ten Commandments open with “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2), and only then do they command. The law was a way of life for a redeemed people, shaped by the holiness of the God who had come to live among them. It was never a ladder by which slaves could climb out of Egypt. It ordered worship and sacrifice, family and property, courts and harvests, and the care of the poor and the foreigner, and it held Israel together as a covenant people (the study on covenant traces the covenants themselves). The New Testament teaches that Christ fulfills the law, and Christians differ on how its parts apply to the church. They agree that it still shows the character of God and every person's need of grace.

The main Hebrew word is torah, which occurs about 220 times in the Old Testament. Its range is wider than the English ‘law’. It can mean a parent's teaching (Proverbs 1:8, where the Berean Standard Bible renders it ‘teaching’), a priest's ruling, a single regulation, the whole book of Moses, and later, among Jews, the five books of Moses and the whole body of God's instruction. ‘Instruction’ often catches its sense better than ‘law’, and the BSB uses that word for the king's copy of it (Deuteronomy 17:18). Beside it stand mitsvah (‘commandment’), choq (‘statute’, a fixed decree), mishpat (‘ordinance’ or ‘judgment’, often a ruling for a case), and ‘edut (‘testimony’), and Psalm 119 plays on the whole vocabulary. The Ten Commandments are called in Hebrew ‘the ten words’ (Deuteronomy 4:13). The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, rendered torah with nomos, which appears nearly two hundred times in the New Testament, most often in Romans and Galatians. In Paul nomos usually means the law of Moses, though he also uses it for a principle at work in a person (Romans 7:21-23).
ot:
God's will is known before Sinai. He commands in Eden (Genesis 2:16-17), forbids murder after the flood (Genesis 9:6), and says Abraham kept “My commandments, My statutes, and My laws” (Genesis 26:5). But the law proper begins in the third month after the exodus, when Israel camps before the mountain (Exodus 19:1). The order of Exodus 19 governs everything after it. God first reminds Israel of rescue, “I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself”, then offers covenant, promising that an obedient Israel will be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (19:4-6). The Ten Commandments follow (Exodus 20:1-17; restated in Deuteronomy 5:6-21), written on two tablets “inscribed by the finger of God” (31:18) and kept in the ark. Then comes the Book of the Covenant (Exodus 20:22-23:33), a collection of case laws. Albrecht Alt (1934) distinguished two forms in Israel's law: casuistic law, which states a case and its penalty (‘if a man…’), and apodictic law, the bare command or prohibition (‘you shall not’). Israel's case laws resemble other ancient collections, such as the laws of Hammurabi of Babylon (about 1750 BC), which also rule on an ox that gores. The differences are as telling as the likeness. In Israel God himself speaks the law, not a king; it reaches the heart (‘you shall not covet’); it protects slaves, widows, and foreigners “for you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Exodus 22:21); and “eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (21:24) sets a limit on retribution for the courts, not a license for private revenge.

Leviticus sets the law inside the presence of a holy God. Its sacrifices, purity laws, and priesthood teach Israel how sinful people may live near him, and its refrain is “be holy, because I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). The law provided for its own breaking: sin offerings and the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) were part of it, so grace stood within the law and not only after it. Leviticus 19, in the chapters scholars call the Holiness Code (17-26), sets ritual beside ethics and gives the command Jesus would call second only to love for God, “love your neighbor as yourself” (19:18), extending it to the foreigner as well (19:34). It also promises, “the man who does these things will live by them” (18:5), which in its setting describes the life of the covenant people in the land; Paul later quotes it in a different argument (Galatians 3:12; Romans 10:5).

Deuteronomy gives the law as Moses' last sermons on the plains of Moab, and it shows the law's heart. Its center is the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One. And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). When a child asks what the statutes mean, the father answers with a story, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out” (6:20-21). The commands are given “for your own good” (10:13), and they are Israel's wisdom before the nations (4:6-8). The law is “not too difficult for you or beyond your reach” (30:11), and Moses sets before the people “life and death, blessing and cursing” and urges them to choose life (30:19). The king must copy the law and read it all his life (17:18-19), and the whole people, children and foreigners included, are to hear it read every seven years (31:10-12). Yet Deuteronomy also foresees failure. It commands, “Circumcise your hearts” (10:16), and then promises that after exile God himself will circumcise their hearts (30:6).

The histories judge Israel by this law. Joshua is told to meditate on it “day and night” (Joshua 1:8), and the books of Kings measure each king by it. In about 622 BC, during repairs to the temple under Josiah, the high priest reported, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD” (2 Kings 22:8), and the king tore his clothes when he heard it. Since W. M. L. de Wette's study of 1805 many scholars have identified that book with some form of Deuteronomy; others hold that it was the law of Moses long neglected. The prophets bring no new law. They act as prosecutors of the covenant already made, and when they attack sacrifice (Isaiah 1:13-17; Hosea 6:6; Micah 6:6-8; Jeremiah 7:22-23), they attack worship cut loose from justice and mercy, not the worship the law commanded. They also look past the broken covenant to a new one, in which God says, “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33), and promises, “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27). Isaiah sees the nations streaming to Zion because “the law will go forth from Zion” (Isaiah 2:3).

After the exile the law became the center of Israel's life. Ezra “had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel” (Ezra 7:10), and Levites read it to the people, “explaining it and giving insight” (Nehemiah 8:8). The Psalms had long sung its goodness: the blessed man delights in it (Psalm 1:2), it is “perfect, reviving the soul” and sweeter than honey (19:7-10), and Psalm 119 meditates on it for 176 verses. The prophetic books close with “Remember the law of My servant Moses” (Malachi 4:4). In 167 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus IV forbade circumcision and Sabbath keeping in Judea, and many Jews died rather than break the law (1 Maccabees 1). By Jesus' day Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes disagreed sharply over how to interpret it, but all agreed that Israel's life before God was bound up with it.
nt:
Jesus was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4), and his parents did for him what was customary under it (Luke 2:27). He said, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17), and went on to press the commands inward: anger is judged with murder and lust with adultery (5:21-28). Interpreters describe his fulfilling in different ways: he taught the law's full meaning, he obeyed it perfectly, and he brought it to the goal it pointed toward. Most hold that all three belong together. He named the love of God and the love of neighbor as the two commandments on which “All the Law and the Prophets hang” (Matthew 22:40), rebuked those who tithed herbs while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness” (23:23), and declared that “The Sabbath was made for man” and that “the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27-28). After his teaching that food cannot defile the heart, Mark adds his own comment: “Thus all foods are clean” (Mark 7:19). Jesus spoke with an authority over the law that no rabbi claimed, and the Gospels present that authority as the authority of the one who gave it.

The early church had to work out what the law meant once Gentiles began to believe. Jewish believers in Jerusalem remained “zealous for the law” (Acts 21:20). At the council in Jerusalem, about AD 49, the question was whether Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Peter called that a yoke “that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear” and said all are saved “through the grace of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 15:10-11). James proposed that Gentiles be asked only to abstain from food offered to idols, sexual immorality, strangled meat, and blood (15:20), requirements that echo Leviticus 17-18 and helped Jews and Gentiles share one table.

Paul gives the law its fullest treatment. He insists that “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16). The law came 430 years after the promise to Abraham and cannot cancel it (3:17); it “was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed” (3:19); it was a guardian (the paidagōgos, the household slave who escorted a child to school) until Christ came (3:24-25). Yet Paul will not let the law be called bad. It “merely brings awareness of sin” (Romans 3:20), but “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (7:12). The fault lies in the flesh, the fallen self, and what the law “was powerless to do in that it was weakened by the flesh”, God did by sending his Son, so that “the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (8:3-4). The new covenant promise of the law on the heart is met by the Spirit. Paul can say both “we uphold the law” (3:31) and “Christ is the end of the law” (10:4); the Greek telos can mean ‘end’, ‘goal’, or both, and interpreters divide over which Paul meant. Love fulfills the law (Romans 13:8-10; Galatians 5:14), and Paul calls himself not outside God's law but “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21; compare Galatians 6:2). What Paul meant by “works of the law” has been debated sharply since the 1970s (see the history below and the study on justification).

The other New Testament writers agree in substance from different angles. Hebrews argues that “when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well” (Hebrews 7:12), that “the law is only a shadow of the good things to come” (10:1), and that the new covenant has made the first “obsolete” (8:13). Paul lists food, festivals, and Sabbaths as “a shadow of the things to come” whose substance “belongs to Christ” (Colossians 2:16-17), and says Christ abolished “the law of commandments and decrees” that divided Jew from Gentile (Ephesians 2:15). James, writing to Jewish believers, calls it “the perfect law of freedom” (James 1:25) and “the royal law”, summed up in love of neighbor (2:8). John writes, “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17), which sets the law as God's earlier gift beside his fuller one, and adds that God's commandments “are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). The New Testament thus holds together a real ending, since Christians are not under the Sinai covenant, and a real continuation, since the law's righteousness is fulfilled in those who love. Christians still debate where exactly the line runs.

keyTexts.why: Rescue comes before command. God reminds Israel that he carried them on eagles’ wings, then offers covenant and calls them a kingdom of priests.
The Ten Commandments, prefaced by God's act of redemption. The core of the law, repeated in Deuteronomy 5 and cited throughout the New Testament.
Holiness joined to neighbor love: gleaning for the poor, honest weights, fair courts, and the command to love your neighbor as yourself.
The Shema and the command to love God with all the heart, the charge to teach children, and the law explained to a child by the story of the exodus.
Beyond exile God promises to circumcise hearts; the command is near, in mouth and heart, and Israel is called to choose life.
The Book of the Law is found in the temple under Josiah, and its reading leads to repentance and reform.
The law celebrated as perfect, reviving, radiant, and sweeter than honey. Israel's worship treats God's instruction as a gift.
The promise of a new covenant in which God writes his law on the heart and forgives sin.
Jesus comes to fulfill the Law and the Prophets, and his teaching carries the commands to the heart.
All the Law and the Prophets hang on love for God and love for neighbor.
The Jerusalem council decides that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or take on the law of Moses to belong to the people of God.
The law exposes sin and is holy, righteous, and good; the problem is not the law but sin working through it.
What the law could not do because of the flesh, God did in Christ, so that the law's righteous standard is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit.
The law came after the promise, cannot annul it, and served as a guardian until Christ.
The royal law of love and the unity of the whole law, from a letter that treats the law as the law of freedom.

history:
The early church rejected two opposite answers. The Ebionites, Jewish followers of Jesus described by Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.26.2, about 180), kept the whole law and rejected Paul. Marcion, who taught in Rome around 144, rejected the law and the God who gave it. Between them the church held that the law came from the Father of Jesus Christ and that it had been fulfilled in him. Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (about 155 to 160) called Christ the eternal and final law and argued that circumcision, the Sabbath, and the sacrifices had been given to Israel because of the people's hardness of heart. Irenaeus taught that the Ten Commandments set out the natural law already written on human hearts, which remains for Christians, while much of the rest was a discipline suited to Israel (Against Heresies 4.15-16). Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter (412), written against the Pelagians, read 2 Corinthians 3:6 to mean that the law without grace can only command and condemn, while the Spirit gives what the law commands.

Medieval theology gave the church its most influential scheme. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, questions 98 to 108, about 1270) divided the Old Law into moral, ceremonial, and judicial precepts. The moral precepts belong to the natural law and bind everyone; the ceremonial precepts foreshadowed Christ and ceased with his coming; the judicial precepts governed Israel as a nation and no longer bind, though a people may adopt them. The New Law, Aquinas taught, is chiefly the grace of the Holy Spirit given through faith in Christ. Jewish tradition developed along its own line: the Mishnah (about AD 200) and the Talmuds interpreted the written Torah through the oral Torah, a teaching in the Babylonian Talmud counts 613 commandments (Makkot 23b), and Moses Maimonides codified the whole in his Mishneh Torah (completed about 1180).

The Reformation made the law a central question. Martin Luther taught that rightly distinguishing law and gospel is the heart of theology: the law commands and accuses and drives sinners to Christ, and the gospel gives what the law demands. Melanchthon's Apology of the Augsburg Confession (1531) taught that the law always accuses. After a dispute with Johann Agricola, who taught that the law had no place in preaching repentance to Christians (Luther opposed him in disputations from 1537 to 1540), Melanchthon spoke of a third use of the law as a guide for believers, and the Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577, Article 6) confessed it. John Calvin taught three uses (to show sin, to restrain evil in society, and to guide believers) and called the third the principal use (Institutes 2.7.6-12); he also used the threefold division (4.20.14-16). The Heidelberg Catechism (1563) placed the Ten Commandments in its part on gratitude, the Thirty-Nine Articles (Article 7) said that the ceremonies and civil precepts of Moses do not bind Christians while the moral commandments do, and the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646, chapter 19) confessed the same threefold division at length.

Modern scholarship reopened the questions. Julius Wellhausen's Prolegomena (1878, retitled in 1883) placed the priestly law after the prophets and portrayed later Judaism as a religion of legalism. E. P. Sanders's Paul and Palestinian Judaism (1977) answered that the Judaism of Paul's day was covenantal nomism, in which obedience responded to grace rather than earning it, and James Dunn's 1982 lecture The New Perspective on Paul (published 1983) argued that ‘works of the law’ meant especially the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws, and the Sabbath. Other scholars defended the older reading that Paul was answering any attempt to be right with God by doing what the law requires, notably Stephen Westerholm (Perspectives Old and New on Paul, 2004) and the contributors to Justification and Variegated Nomism (edited by D. A. Carson, Peter O'Brien, and Mark Seifrid, 2001 and 2004). A Qumran text known as 4QMMT uses a Hebrew phrase close to Paul's ‘works of the law’ for its own rulings, and both sides cite it. Among evangelicals, the book Five Views on Law and Gospel (1996) set out Reformed, theonomic, dispensational, and modified Lutheran positions side by side.

differ.view: The threefold division (Reformed, Anglican, and much Catholic teaching)
differ.body: The law of Moses contains moral, ceremonial, and civil precepts. The ceremonial laws, sacrifices, priesthood, food laws, and festivals were shadows of Christ and are fulfilled in him (Colossians 2:17; Hebrews 10:1). The civil laws governed Israel as a nation and expired with that nation, though their underlying justice still instructs. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, reflects God's own character and was written on the heart at creation (Romans 2:14-15), so it binds all people in every age. Jesus and the apostles cite the commandments as still in force (Romans 13:9), and Jeremiah's new covenant writes God's law on the heart rather than removing it. Aquinas, Calvin, the Thirty-Nine Articles, and the Westminster Confession teach this view, and Willem VanGemeren and Walter Kaiser defended forms of it in Five Views on Law and Gospel.

The decisive distinction in Scripture is between two words God speaks: the law, which commands and accuses, and the gospel, which promises and gives. The law shows sinners their need and drives them to Christ (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:24), and it restrains evil in the world. For believers it remains a guide, since they are still sinners as well as saints, but it never becomes the ground of their standing before God, and preaching that mixes the two robs consciences of comfort. Luther, Melanchthon, and the Formula of Concord shaped this view, and C. F. W. Walther's lectures on the proper distinction between law and gospel carried it into American Lutheranism. Douglas Moo defended a modified form in Five Views on Law and Gospel.

differ.view: The law of Christ (new covenant theology and related views)
differ.body: The law of Moses was given to Israel as a single covenant package and cannot be divided into parts that remain and parts that expire. The whole of it reached its goal in Christ (Romans 10:4), and the first covenant is now obsolete (Hebrews 8:13). Believers are not under the law of Moses but “under the law of Christ” (1 Corinthians 9:21), the will of God taught by Jesus and his apostles. Nine of the Ten Commandments are repeated in the New Testament and bind Christians, but as Christ's commands. The Old Testament law remains Scripture and teaches believers wisdom, but it is read through Christ. Proponents include Tom Wells and Fred Zaspel, and Moo's position has much in common with it.

The Mosaic law was the rule of life for Israel in a particular dispensation, from Sinai to the cross, and it ended with Christ's death (Galatians 3:19, 25). The church lives under grace in a new administration, guided by the teaching of Christ and the apostles and empowered by the Spirit. The moral content of the law reappears in the New Testament, but Christians obey it because it is repeated there, not because Sinai binds them. Classic dispensationalists drew this line sharply; later dispensationalists, such as Wayne Strickland in Five Views on Law and Gospel, describe the law of Christ as the inaugurated rule of the new covenant.

God's law, including the civil laws given to Israel and their penalties, remains the standard of justice for every nation unless the New Testament changes it, since Jesus said that not a stroke of a pen will disappear from the law (Matthew 5:18). The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ, but the moral and judicial laws abide in their general equity, and civil governments today should be measured by them. R. J. Rushdoony (The Institutes of Biblical Law, 1973) and Greg Bahnsen (Theonomy in Christian Ethics, 1977) are its main advocates. It remains a minority position, and most Reformed churches, while holding the threefold division, reject it.

errors:
Two errors the church has rejected from the beginning lie on either side of the truth. Legalism treats the law as the way sinners earn God's favor. It turns the order of Exodus upside down, as if God had given the commandments in Egypt and promised rescue to those who kept them. The Jerusalem council rejected it (Acts 15:10-11), and Paul fought it in Galatians because it made Christ's death pointless (Galatians 2:21). Antinomianism, from the Greek for ‘against law’, holds that because believers are saved by grace, God's commands have no claim on them. Paul answered it in the same letters (Romans 6:1-2; Galatians 5:13-14), Luther opposed it in his disputations against Agricola, and the church has consistently held that grace produces obedience rather than cancelling it.

The church has also rejected Marcion's claim that the law came from a lesser god, and it has had to repent of a long habit of caricaturing Judaism as a religion of cold legalism. The Psalms' delight in the law, the law's own provision of sacrifice and forgiveness, and the Jewish scholarship that shaped the modern study of Paul all stand against that caricature, whatever one concludes about Paul's argument. A third distortion reduces the law to rules for private morality and forgets its concern for justice. The law protected the foreigner, the widow, and the orphan, left the edges of the field for the poor (Deuteronomy 24:19), and limited the powerful, and the prophets held Israel to all of it.
life:
The order of Exodus, rescue first and then command, shapes how a Christian hears every command in Scripture. God's commands are not the price of his love but the shape of life with him, which is why the psalmists could love his law and pray it. The law still does what Paul said it does: it shows sin honestly, and so it sends people back to Christ again and again. It also keeps obedience concrete. Love of neighbor in the law means honest scales, fair wages paid on time, a share of the harvest left for the poor, and care for the stranger, and Jesus sums the law up in love without dissolving it into a feeling.

For the believer the promise of the new covenant is the law written on the heart by the Spirit. That means the Christian life is neither anxious rule keeping nor indifference to what God has said, but a growing desire to do his will. Reading the law with that in view changes the long chapters of Leviticus and Deuteronomy from a burden into a window on God's holiness, his mercy, and his concern for every part of human life.
questions: God rescued Israel from Egypt before he gave the law at Sinai. How does that order change the way you hear the commands of Scripture?
Paul says the law is holy, righteous, and good, and also that Christ is the end of the law. How do the different Christian views in this study hold those two statements together?
The law cared for the poor, the foreigner, the widow, and the orphan. What would it look like for a church or a household to take those parts of the law seriously today?
